lesson.title: Kleidung II: die Socke, die Tasche, die Mütze, der Schal, der Hut
lesson.subtitle: the small gear — two Latin loans, one word Germany borrowed back from English, and two honest losses

hook.title: Words That Travel in Both Directions
hook.content: Kleidung I gave you four English twins; the small gear tells a messier, more human story. die Socke and English sock are the same Latin word, soccus — the light slipper Roman comic actors wore — which walked into both Germanic languages separately. der Schal travelled the wrong way: Germany borrowed it FROM English shawl (which itself started life in Persian). der Hut is the honest ancient twin of hat, straight from Proto-Germanic *hattuz. And then two honest losses: die Tasche and die Mütze have no safe English twin — English lost those words somewhere in the last thousand years, and pretending otherwise would be fabrication. Borrowing is a two-way street: German lent and borrowed, and the wardrobe keeps the receipts.

footnotes.title: The Slipper of Roman Comedy
footnotes.content: Latin soccus was the low, slipper-like shoe worn by the actors of Roman comedy — the sock of 'sock and buskin', the old phrase for comedy and tragedy. English sock and German Socke both take their word from that stage floor.

pattern.title: Tragen Takes an Object
pattern.content: Three frames. 1. tragen + accusative: Ich trage einen Schal (masc.), eine Mütze (fem.), einen Hut — the clothing is the object, so einen/eine ride along: Ich trage den Regenmantel. 2. Position with dative: Der Schal ist über dem Hemd (the scarf is over the shirt) — über + dem for where something hangs. 3. Inside-compounds: Die Tasche ist im Mantel (the bag is in the coat), Meine Nummer ist in der Tasche. And the compound engine from Kleidung I keeps running: der Regenmantel is literally der Regen + der Mantel, a rain-coat for the rain.
pattern.linguist_note: English 'shawl' entered from Persian shāl via India in the 18th century and was so fashionable that German borrowed it right back as der Schal — a reverse loan, the linguistic equivalent of re-exporting a fashion.

exercises.prompt: The small gear, in position — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The sock and the shoe belong together
The scarf is over the shirt
matching_pairs.german: Der Schal ist über dem Hemd

matching_pairs.english: The bag is in the coat
My number is in the bag
matching_pairs.german: Meine Nummer ist in der Tasche

matching_pairs.english: The jacket is new, the trousers are old
matching_pairs.german: Die Jacke ist neu, die Hose ist alt

matching_pairs.english: The rain-coat is for the rain
matching_pairs.german: Der Regenmantel ist für den Regen

exercises.target_answer: Die Socke und der Schuh, Der Schal ist über dem Hemd, Die Tasche ist im Mantel, Meine Nummer ist in der Tasche, Die Jacke ist neu, die Hose ist alt, Der Regenmantel ist für den Regen
exercises.meaning: socks and shoes, scarves over shirts, bags inside coats, a rain-coat for the rain
exercises.explanation: Six positions, one wardrobe. über dem Hemd is dative because the scarf merely hangs there; für den Regen is accusative because the coat is destined for it. And die Socke pairs with der Schuh — two genders the English words never had to learn.

exercises.prompt: One of these words travelled the wrong way: Germany took IT from English. Which?
exercises.meaning: der Schal is a reverse loan: German took it FROM English
exercises.explanation: der Schal came from English shawl in the 19th century, when shawls were the height of fashion. die Socke and English sock both borrowed separately from Latin soccus, and der Hut ↔ hat is an ancient Germanic twin — but only the Schal crossed from English into German.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the pair that belongs together: 'The sock and the shoe'
exercises.explanation: die Socke, der Schuh — the article rides with the noun, and und simply stacks them. das Hemd sits in the bank to prove the article changes with the noun: das Hemd, die Socke, der Schuh.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The jacket is new and the trousers are old'
exercises.target_answer: Die Jacke ist neu und die Hose ist alt
exercises.meaning: The jacket is new and the trousers are old
exercises.explanation: One und, two clauses. die Jacke and die Hose are both feminine, so the same article fronts each noun — the contrast between neu and alt carries the whole sentence.

exercises.idea: you are getting dressed and announce what goes on top: you are wearing the hat and the cap
cues: der Hut becomes den Hut (masculine accusative); die Mütze stays die Mütze
exercises.target_answer: Ich trage den Hut und die Mütze
exercises.meaning: I am wearing the hat and the cap
exercises.explanation: tragen is the wardrobe's verb: Ich trage den Hut (masc. → den), die Mütze (fem. → die). The masculine is the only one that changes its article in the accusative — the feminine and neuter stay put.

diagnosis.slip: the masculine article stayed der in the accusative
diagnosis.cue: Only the masculine changes: der Hut → den Hut. die Mütze and das Hemd keep their articles in every case you will meet this week.

summary.outcome: Talk about the small gear, put a scarf over a shirt and a bag in a coat — and know which words Germany borrowed, lent, and lost.

use_example.german: Der Schal ist über dem Hemd — ich trage den Hut und die Mütze.
use_example.english: The scarf is over the shirt — I am wearing the hat and the cap.

summary.takeaway: Socke and sock share Latin soccus, der Schal is a loan FROM English shawl, der Hut is hat's ancient twin — and die Tasche, die Mütze stand alone, honestly.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the rooms you live in — das Zimmer, die Wohnung, der Flur, der Keller, die Etage — and the word hiding inside English timber.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Kleidung II: die Socke, die Tasche, die Mütze, der Schal, der Hut (The jacket is new and the trousers are old):
twist.target_answer: Die Jacke ist neu und die Hose ist alt
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Jacke ist neu und die Hose ist alt" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Kleidung II: die Socke, die Tasche, die Mütze, der Schal, der Hut without relying on short-term echo.

socke.etymology_derivation: West Germanic borrowing from Latin soccus 'slipper' — a parallel borrowing with English sock. [wiktionary]

tasche.etymology_derivation: Perhaps Proto-Germanic *taskǭ; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

mütze.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin almutia 'hood, cowl' — a Romance loan; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

schal.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English shawl, from Persian šâl — a loan, not an inherited cognate. [wiktionary]

hut.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hōdaz — Wiktionary's English cognate is hood, not hat. See Fingerhut. [wiktionary]

nummer.etymology_derivation: From Italian numero, from Latin numerus — the same Latin word that gives English number. [wiktionary]

schuh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *skōh — the true twin of English shoe (see Handschuh, hand-shoe). [wiktionary]

hose.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hosā — the same Germanic source as English hose (hosiery). [wiktionary]

hemd.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi; English shirt is from a different root — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

mantel.etymology_derivation: From Late Latin mantellum, ultimately Gaulish — a Romance loan; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

jacke.etymology_derivation: From Middle French jaque (from the name Jacques) — the same French source as English jacket. [wiktionary]

tragen.etymology_derivation: Class 6 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *draganą (to carry, drag) - the twin of English draw and drag; tragen-trug-getragen matches draw-drew-drawn. [wiktionary]

hase.context_phrase: Der Hase springt über das Feld.
hase.context_translation: The hare jumps over the field.
hase.etymology_derivation: From Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from an old root meaning grey. English hare belongs to the same Germanic grey-word family. [wiktionary]

ferien.context_phrase: Im Sommer haben wir sechs Wochen Ferien.
ferien.context_translation: In summer we have six weeks of holidays.
ferien.etymology_derivation: Plural-only word from Latin feriae, days of rest and festival, with the Latin plural ending replaced by German -en. [wiktionary]

heben.context_translation: Do not lift such heavy boxes.
heben.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *habbjan — English heave is the documented cognate (Dutch heffen); strong verb: hob, gehoben. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
